sentences.text: Jiangxisuchus was a small to medium-sized crocodylian with a short, blunt snout.
The name Jiangxisuchus combines the Jiangxi Province of China with the Greek suffix -suchus, meaning crocodile.
Its snout was short and blunt, similar to that of the extinct genus Stangerochampsa.
A prominent notch in the snout contributes to the pronounced festooning, or sinuous appearance, of the jaw in Jiangxisuchus.
The skull featured large eyesockets with raised rims that were larger than any other openings on the head.
The lower jaw met at a relatively short symphysis formed entirely by dentary bones, ending just after the fifth tooth socket.
In the upper jaw, the third premaxillary tooth was the largest, while the first was the smallest.
The fifth maxillary tooth was the largest in the upper jaw, followed by the fourth and eleventh.
The first nine upper teeth were conical, unserrated, and slightly curved.
From the tenth tooth onward, the upper teeth had constricted bases and low, bean-shaped crowns.
The lower jaw of Jiangxisuchus contained 19 teeth in total.
The fourth lower tooth was the largest, and the twelfth was likely the second largest.
Bony septums separated some lower jaw teeth, and a gap existed between the eighth and ninth lower teeth.
Evidence suggests Jiangxisuchus had armored limbs, indicated by an elliptical osteoderm lacking a crest.
Jiangxisuchus was described in 2019 by Chun Li, Xiao-Chun Wu, and Scott James Rufolo as the first crocodilian found in the Cretaceous Nanxiong Formation of Nankang, China.
The genus Jiangxisuchus was named by Li and colleagues in 2019.
The type species of the genus Jiangxisuchus is Jiangxisuchus nankangensis.
Eurycephalosuchus, a close relative of Jiangxisuchus, is characterized by a very short snout.
When described in 2019, Jiangxisuchus was initially proposed to be a basal member of the group Crocodyloidea.
A concurrent 2019 study placed Jiangxisuchus in the clade Orientalosuchina, suggesting it was an early alligatoroid.
The scientific classification of Jiangxisuchus has remained uncertain since its initial description.
Scientists disagree on whether Jiangxisuchus is a crocodyloid or an alligatoroid and its exact relationship to orientalosuchins.
Some studies place Jiangxisuchus as the closest relative to the early Paleocene species Eoalligator chunyii.
Later studies still found Jiangxisuchus and Eoalligator to be sister taxa, though the rest of the group's relationships shifted.
While many studies group Jiangxisuchus with Orientalosuchina as early alligatoroids, this classification is contested.
A 2021 study by Rio and Manion classified Jiangxisuchus as an early crocodyloid rather than an alligatoroid.
In conflicting studies, Jiangxisuchus was consistently found to be closer to crocodiles and gharials than to alligatoroids.
A 2023 study by Ristevski et al. proposed an intermediate classification placing Jiangxisuchus within the Australian group Mekosuchinae.
The hypothesis that Orientalosuchina belongs within Mekosuchinae has weak support due to few shared unique traits.
Jiangxisuchus belongs to the crocodilian group Longirostres.
Jiangxisuchus is classified as a reptile.
Jiangxisuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Maastrichtian stage.
Jiangxisuchus lived in a subhumid environment near the base of an alluvial fan influenced by rivers.
The geological age of the Hekou Formation, where Jiangxisuchus fossils were found, is typically accepted as Maastrichtian, though some studies suggest a range from Coniacian to Santonian.
Jiangxisuchus lived between 72.2 and 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage.
